topics.topic: The Machine the Entire Chip Industry Depends On
topics.coreQuestion: Why does the most advanced chipmaking run through one company's tin-plasma light machine?
topics.dependency: Leading-edge chips at 5 and 3 nanometre process nodes depend on EUV exposure steps.
topics.mechanism: A laser hits falling tin droplets to make a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light; mirrors in vacuum carry it to a reflective photomask.
topics.bottleneck: A single supplier builds the complete system, and its tin-plasma source and vacuum mirror optics have no drop-in substitute.
topics.failureConsequence: Without new EUV tools or service, fabs could not add leading-edge capacity; installed tools keep running only as long as maintenance and spares allow.
topics.resilience: Service contracts, spare modules and slower multi-exposure deep-UV patterning are the fallbacks while alternative sources are developed.
topics.openingLine: Every advanced chip depends on one machine.
topics.secondBeat: Only one company builds and sells it.
topics.expectedConsequence: leading-edge capacity stalls first; mature-node chips are largely unaffected

researchEvidence.claim: EUV lithography uses 13.5 nm extreme ultraviolet light from a laser-pulsed tin plasma.
As of 2025, ASML is the only company that produces and sells EUV systems for chip production, targeting 5 nm and 3 nm process nodes.
The light source ejects molten tin droplets about 25 μm across at about 70 m/s through a vacuum chamber.
EUV light is absorbed by glass and air, so the systems use mirrors in vacuum instead of lenses.
Earlier deep-UV lithography used 193 nm light from argon fluoride lasers.

narration.text: Every advanced chip depends on one machine.
Only one company builds and sells it.
It uses extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nanometres.

narration.text: Why 6% leftover heat nearly melted a reactor.
In 1979, Three Mile Island's reactor shut down automatically.

Coolant drained away, and the core partly melted.
Cleanup lasted until 1993 and cost about $1 billion.
That's why cooling after shutdown matters as much as control.

facts.claim: Emissions from cement kilns are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for around 2.5% of non-natural carbon emissions worldwide.
The emissions come from two sources: the fuel and the waste CO2 created from heating the silicate rocks.
900 to 1050 °C – the remaining calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide (CaO) and CO2.
Typically, a peak temperature of 1400–1450 °C is required to complete the reaction.
The hot clinker next falls into a cooler which recovers most of its heat, and cools the clinker to around 100 °C.

narration.text: Every bridge starts in a 1,450 °C kiln.
Cement kilns emit about 2.5% of human-made carbon.
Limestone releases CO2 as it breaks down near 900 °C.
So even clean fuel can't remove all the emissions.
At 1,400 to 1,450 °C, the minerals partly melt into clinker.
A cooler then brings clinker down to around 100 °C.
Stop the kiln, and concrete supply for whole regions stalls.
That's why the hardest emissions to cut are chemical, not fuel.

facts.claim: Around 450-500 million EUR-pallets are in circulation.
The weight of a EUR/EPAL-pallet (EPAL 1) is approximately 25 kg.

narration.text: Why 500 million pallets share one size.
European railways standardised the EUR-pallet in 1961.
Each weighs about 25 kilograms.
It safely carries 1,500 kilograms.
Stacked, it can bear up to 4,000 kilograms more.
Around 450 to 500 million are in circulation.
When pallets run short, loading docks slow down.
That's why a wooden standard keeps Europe's freight moving.

narration.text: Why 42 countries vet each other's tech exports.

It replaced a Cold War system that blocked the Eastern Bloc.

Members agree lists of dual-use goods that need licences.
A new listing can halt shipments of chips or tools overnight.
That's why paperwork shapes the global tech supply chain.

narration.text: Why the master kilogram lost 50 micrograms.
It drifted compared with its own copies over a century.
It was checked only three times: 1889, 1948 and 1989.
Nations kept platinum-iridium copies to calibrate against it.
If the master drifts, every scale in the chain drifts with it.
So in 2019, the kilogram was redefined by a constant of nature.
That's why no metal object defines a kilogram anymore.

narration.text: Why the internet's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.
IPv4 was designed long before phones and smart devices.

Back then, only 16 to 26% of computers could use IPv6.
So networks began sharing addresses behind translators.
That's why a numbering standard still shapes how you connect.

topics.topic: The Liquid Helium Keeping MRI Magnets Cold
topics.coreQuestion: Why do MRI scanners depend on a liquid that exists only four degrees above absolute zero?
topics.dependency: Superconducting MRI magnets depend on liquid helium to stay cold enough to superconduct.

editorialTitles: Where the World's E-Waste Goes
Why Most Old Electronics Aren't Recycled

facts.claim: In 2022, approximately 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were generated globally; only 22.3% were formally collected and recycled.
Global e-waste generation is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030.
Around 70% of toxic waste in landfills is electronic waste, even though e-waste accounts for only 3% of the waste in landfills.
A 2011 report found that of 215,000 tons of electronics imported to Ghana, 30% was brand new and 70% was used.

narration.text: Why only 22.3% of e-waste gets recycled.
The world generated about 62 million tonnes in 2022.
That's projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030.
E-waste is 3% of landfill waste, but 70% of its toxic waste.
Smelters can recover metals only from what gets collected.
Everything else leaks value and toxins.
That's why collection, not technology, limits e-waste recycling.
